content: Speech communication involves the processes related to the production and perception of sounds used in spoken language. Various academic fields, such as acoustics, psychology, speech pathology, linguistics, and computer science, study different aspects of speech and speech sounds. In the field of linguistics, particularly in articulatory phonetics, the term manner of articulation refers to the way in which the tongue, lips, and other speech organs interact to produce specific sounds. This concept is primarily applied to the production of consonants. For a given place of articulation, there can be multiple manners of articulation, resulting in the production of several consonants that share the same place of articulation. Speech perception is the process by which humans interpret and comprehend the sounds used in spoken language. This area of study is closely associated with phonetics and phonology in linguistics, as well as cognitive psychology and sensory perception in psychology. Research in speech perception aims to understand how listeners recognize speech sounds and use this information to derive meaning from spoken language. This research has practical applications, such as developing computer systems capable of recognizing speech and improving speech recognition technologies for individuals with hearing or language impairments. Several biological and psychological factors can negatively impact speech. These include: Disorders or diseases affecting the lungs or vocal cords, such as vocal cord paralysis, respiratory infections, vocal fold nodules, and cancers of the lungs or throat. Neurological conditions affecting the brain, such as alogia, aphasias, dysarthria, dystonia, and speech processing disorders. These conditions may impair motor planning, nerve transmission, phonological processing, or the perception of the intended message, leading to difficulties in speech production. Hearing issues, such as otitis media with effusion, can result in phonological problems. Articulatory challenges, including stuttering, lisping, cleft palate, ataxia, or nerve damage, can interfere with the ability to articulate speech sounds properly. Conditions like Tourette syndrome and tics can also disrupt speech. Beyond aphasias, conditions such as anomia and certain forms of dyslexia can impair auditory perception and, consequently, speech expression. Hearing impairments and deafness also fall into this category, as they can significantly affect both the perception and production of speech.
